title: Socinians: God's government and the inward act
source_text: LXXXV. Quod si quis objiciat, si res ita se habet, multum de Dei gubernatione, quae in mundo regendo cernitur, detractum iri: respondent, internum voluntatis nostrae actum, quem solum ordinarie in nostra potestate Deus collocavit, in mundi gubernatione nullum habere momentum, sed externum ejus effectum, qui in Dei potestate ita situs est, ut nihil nisi Deo decernente, juvanteque, aut permittente fieri queat. Liberum autem arbitrium eousque vim suam porrigere, ut Deo nunc juvante, nunc permittente tantum, homo non solum de re quapiam peragenda cogitationem suscipere, sed etiam exitu eam complere possit.
pass_a_gloss: LXXXV. But if anyone objects, if the matter is so, that much will be taken away from the government of God, which is seen in ruling the world: they answer, that the internal act of our will, which alone God has ordinarily placed in our power, has no weight in the government of the world, but its external effect does, which is so placed in God's power, that nothing can be done except with God decreeing, & helping, or permitting. But that free choice extends its force so far, that with God now helping, now only permitting, man can not only undertake the thought of carrying out some thing, but also complete it in outcome.
pass_b_english: Thesis LXXXV. If anyone objects that on this view much will be taken away from God's government as seen in his ruling of the world, they answer that the inward act of our will, the only thing God has ordinarily put in our power, carries no weight in the government of the world.

What matters there is its outward effect, which is so subject to God's power that nothing can happen unless God decrees and helps, or permits it. Free choice reaches far enough, they say, that with God sometimes helping and sometimes only permitting, a person can not only conceive a plan to do something but carry it through to the end.
